extracted.intended_audience: readers of Rabelais and general readers of satirical/humorous Renaissance literature
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and authorial prefatory remarks on how to read and interpret Rabelais' Gargantua — advises readers not to judge by outward titles, to seek deeper/allegorical meanings, and defends mirth as a legitimate purpose of the work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not judge a work by its title or outward appearance
rubrics_metrics.description: Open the book, and seriously consider of the matter treated in it. Then shall you find that it containeth things of far higher value than the box did promise; that is to say, that the subject thereof is not so foolish as by the title at the first sight it would appear to be.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Author warns readers against superficially rejecting books because of playful or mocking titles; just as clothing does not make the monk, appearance (the title) need not reflect the work's substance. Readers should 'open the book' and investigate the content before judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: When literal sense is merry, seek a sublimer/allegorical interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: Yet must not you stop there as at the melody of the charming syrens, but endeavour to interpret that in a sublimer sense which possibly you intended to have spoken in the jollity of your heart.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if passages read as mere jest or recreation, readers are urged to look for higher meanings or allegories behind the jollity. The author explicitly invites allegorical extraction from seemingly simple or bawdy material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Read sedulously and meditate to extract the work's 'marrow'
rubrics_metrics.description: You must, by a sedulous lecture, and frequent meditation, break the bone, and suck out the marrow,--that is, my allegorical sense ... in the perusal of this treatise you shall find another kind of taste, and a doctrine of a more profound and abstruse consideration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author uses the image of breaking a bone and sucking the marrow to advise slow, attentive reading and repeated reflection to uncover deeper doctrinal, religious, political, and moral meanings concealed within the comic surface.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adopt a charitable/beneficent interpretation of the author's words
rubrics_metrics.description: Therefore interpret you all my deeds and sayings in the perfectest sense; reverence the cheese-like brain that feeds you with these fair billevezees and trifling jollities, and do what lies in you to keep me always merry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Readers are asked to take the author's statements in the best possible light (charitable reading), preserving the spirit of merriment and avoiding malicious or depraved constructions of the text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reading for mirth is legitimate and valuable
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Tis true that it brings forth to you no birth Of any value, but in point of mirth; ... One inch of joy surmounts of grief a span; Because to laugh is proper to the man.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author affirms that generating mirth is a valid purpose of literature; readers should not be offended by jocular content and should acknowledge the psychological/social value of laughter and amusement.

rubrics_metrics.name: The convivial hour is a fitting time to compose high matters
rubrics_metrics.description: And indeed that is the fittest and most proper hour wherein to write these high matters and deep sciences: as Homer knew very well ... although a certain sneaking jobernol alleged that his verses smelled more of the wine than oil.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author defends composing significant or learned material in convivial contexts (while eating/drinking), suggesting such hours can produce worthy writing despite critics who disparage the practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be skeptical of retrospective allegorical claims about earlier authors
rubrics_metrics.description: Do you believe, upon your conscience, that Homer ... had any thought upon those allegories, which Plutarch, Heraclides Ponticus, Eustathius, Cornutus squeezed out of him ... If you trust it, with neither hand nor foot do you come near to my opinion, which judgeth them to have been as little dreamed of by Homer ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author cautions against confidently asserting that past authors consciously encoded later-extracted allegories; one should not uncritically accept scholars who retroject allegorical readings onto earlier texts. (This is offered alongside the invitation for readers themselves to search for meanings.)
